editorial.headline: Apartment Hotels in Bali: Open Nationally, Clear of the Moratorium
editorial.standfirst: This classification covers public short-stay apartment hotels, open to PMA nationwide and not barred by Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
Apartment hotel activity is the business of providing short-term accommodation to the public by managing and operating apartments as hotels for temporary stays. It puts the emphasis on the service delivered to guests: accommodation is offered to the public, but through a hotel function within apartment units. The record makes that operational character central. An apartment becomes part of this activity when it is managed and made to function as a hotel for temporary residents, rather than being regarded solely by its property form. The temporary-stay element is expressly part of the description, placing guests rather than long-term occupants at the centre of the accommodation.

That definition leaves a useful boundary in plain sight. The scope speaks of payment being calculated under the applicable arrangements and gives hotel apartments and condominium hotels—often known as apartel or condotel—as its examples. The classification follows the operating model: apartments are managed and functioned as hotel lodging for temporary stays. For an operator, that is the critical description to carry through every conversation about the business: not simply apartments, but apartments placed into hotel operation for the public. It is this service-led use that identifies the activity.

Registration is open to businesses at every listed scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar. That full-range treatment gives the classification a notably broad place in hotel accommodation. No one of these listed scales is set apart as the sole entry point; all four appear in the record as open. The practical reading is that the same defined hotel-apartment activity has a recognised place from Mikro through Besar, while the scope itself remains constant: public short-term accommodation operated in the manner of a hotel. That breadth relates to the scale range, not to a different activity.

Nationally, the PMA status is TERBUKA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100%. Bali does not undo that national position. The Bali entry is not blocked and classifies the position as OK or higher risk. Its stated reason is specific: at Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi—Medium-High/High—meaning this activity is not blocked by the moratorium. The distinction matters because Bali’s permanent, island-wide rule blocks PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. The conclusion here is therefore not a Bali-side prohibition. On the facts in the record, foreign investors may register this activity in Bali through PMA; the record places it outside the moratorium’s blocked risk range.
